questions.q: How is an alert fundamentally different from a job's own failure notification?
options: An alert is a standalone trigger that fires on a specific SQL Server error number, severity level, or performance condition, independent of whether any job was even involved — while a job's own notification fires only when that specific job fails
An alert and a job's failure notification are the same object with two different names
An alert can only be triggered manually by a DBA, never automatically
A job's failure notification fires on any error anywhere on the server, while alerts only fire for that one job
questions.explain: Alerts fire on raw engine conditions (e.g. a severity 19+ error) that no job needs to be running for; job notification is scoped to that job's own outcome.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is severity 19 treated as a meaningful threshold for alerts?
options: Severity 19 and above represents resource errors and internal-consistency errors serious enough to require immediate DBA attention, not just logging
Severity 19 is the maximum severity level SQL Server can generate
Severity 19 only applies to SQL Server Agent job failures, not engine errors
Severity 19 alerts are purely informational and require no action
questions.explain: This is the real line Microsoft's documentation treats as needing immediate attention, which is why the lesson's example alert targets it.

questions.q: What is an operator in SQL Server Agent's model?
options: Agent's representation of who receives a notification — a person, distribution list, or (in practice today) a webhook-routed target — historically including pager support
A T-SQL function that transforms alert messages before sending
A type of job step used exclusively for PowerShell commands
A database role that grants permission to create jobs
questions.explain: The operator object model hasn't changed even as the actual delivery mechanism moved from pagers toward email and webhook/Teams/Slack routing.

questions.q: Why would a production maintenance strategy typically wire both job-level notification and severity-based alerts to the same operator?
options: Because job-level notification covers the routine maintenance work that was scheduled, while severity-based alerts cover serious conditions that weren't scheduled but still need immediate attention
Because SQL Server requires both to be configured before any notification will ever be sent
Because alerts and job notifications always duplicate the exact same information
Because only one of the two can be active at any given time
questions.explain: The two mechanisms cover different scopes — planned job outcomes versus unplanned severe conditions — so a complete strategy uses both.

questions.q: What does sp_add_notification actually connect, per the example in this lesson?
options: A specific alert to a specific operator and notification method (e.g. email)
A job step to a schedule
A resource pool to a workload group
A database to its compatibility level
questions.explain: sp_add_notification is the piece that ties an already-created alert to an already-created operator, specifying how that operator is notified.
